excerpt: Using your bank's USSD code to check a balance, send money, or buy airtime when data is gone, and the reference number to keep afterwards.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to bank without the internet, using the USSD code your bank gives you. You will check a balance, send money, buy airtime, and keep the reference number. It works on the cheapest phone, with no data at all.

USSD is the menu that appears when you dial a short code, like a text conversation with the bank. It runs on the phone network rather than the internet, which is why it still works when data is finished.
Before you start

items: The SIM registered to your bank account, in the phone.
Your bank's USSD code, printed on its website or the back of your card.
Some airtime, since most sessions cost a small amount.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Find the right code

items: Look on the back of your debit card, which usually prints the code.
Or check the bank's own website, on the page for USSD banking.
Or call the bank's customer line and ask them to read it out.
Do not use a code sent to you in a message, even if it looks official.
Save the code in your contacts under the bank's name, so you cannot forget it.
Note that a code from another bank will not work on your account.

body.text: You will see a menu appear in a grey box on the screen, with numbered options and a box for your reply. The whole session looks plain, which is what makes it work on any handset.

body.alt: A phone screen showing a USSD menu with numbered options.
body.caption: Numbered options and a reply box. The menu answers when you type a number, and the session ends when you close it.

body.text: It looks like the session is unsafe because it looks old. It runs on the network's own channel, tied to your SIM, and the danger is only in sharing your PIN or your code with a person.
A session, step by step

items: Dial the code and wait for the menu, which can take ten seconds.
Choose the option for the task, such as balance or transfer.
Type the amount, then the account number, and check both before confirming.
Enter your PIN when the menu asks, and never before.
Read the confirmation on screen, including the reference number.
Close the session by pressing cancel, rather than leaving it open.

body.text: The confirmation will show a reference number and the amount, and it often arrives as a text message too. That number is what the bank will ask for if the money does not arrive.

body.alt: A phone showing an SMS alert from a bank after a USSD transaction.
body.caption: The text alert is the record. Keep it until the person confirms the money arrived, then delete it in your own time.

body.text: Keep the reference

items: Screenshot the confirmation, since the menu disappears when you close it.
Write the reference number on paper if the screenshot is unclear.
Keep the SMS alert, which arrives within a minute.
Check the receiver's account before sending a second time.
Note the charge, which is usually small but appears on the statement.
If the transaction fails, the reference proves you tried.

body.text: None of this needs data or a smartphone. A phone with a keypad, a registered SIM, and a little airtime is enough for all of it.
Do not worry about the menu timing out. Dial again, and the session starts fresh; a half-finished transfer either completes or does not, and the alert tells you which.

body.alt: A notebook with a written transaction reference number and a date.
body.caption: A reference number on paper survives a flat battery. Write it before you put the phone away.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and the alert is the first thing to check.

items: The menu does not appear: the SIM is not the registered one, or the network is busy.
The session ends mid-transfer: wait for the alert before trying again.
The money left but did not arrive: call the bank with the reference number.
You typed the wrong account number: call the bank at once, since recovery is possible but slow.
A caller asks for your PIN to reverse a transfer: refuse, and end the call.
The code is rejected: it may have changed. Check the bank's page again.

body.text: Practice
Do one harmless session today, so the second one is calm.

items: Dial the code and choose the balance option.
Read the menu to the end without choosing anything.
Buy a small amount of airtime for your own number.
Screenshot the confirmation.
Write the code in your notebook, with the bank's name.

body.text: You can now move money when the data is gone. In the next lesson you will find and stop the charges that eat your airtime.

excerpt: Finding the subscriptions that take airtime every week, how to stop them, and how to get a refund when a service was added without you.

body.text: This lesson is about the small charges that disappear from your airtime every week. You will learn how to find them, how to stop them, and what to do when a service was added without your agreement.

Value-added services are subscriptions sold through the network: ringtones, text alerts, games, and quizzes. They charge a small amount daily or weekly, and the total across a year is often surprising.
Before you start

items: The phone with the SIM.
The network's customer line, saved in contacts.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Find what is being charged

items: Read the text messages from the network, since each charge sends one.
Look for messages that name a service and an amount, not only a balance.
Check the network's app, which usually lists active subscriptions.
Dial the network's code for managing services, if one is printed on its site.
Call the customer line and ask what is active on the line.
Write down each service, its amount, and how often it charges.

body.text: You will see the list is often three or four services, each charging a few naira a day. Added together, they explain the airtime that vanishes without a call being made.

body.alt: A phone showing a text message naming a subscription charge.
body.caption: The charge message names the service. Read these messages rather than deleting them, since they are the receipt.

body.text: It looks like the charges come from the network alone. Most are from third-party services the network bills for, which is why the network can stop them and refund them.
Stop them properly

items: Use the network's own stop command, which is printed on its site for each service.
Or ask the customer line to deactivate every value-added service on the line.
Ask for a confirmation message, and keep it.
Check again after two days, since some services take a day to stop.
Do not reply STOP to a promotional message from an unknown short code, which sometimes confirms the number.
Block promotional messages from the network's settings if the option exists.

body.text: The confirmation will name the service and say it has been deactivated, with a date. That message is the proof if a charge appears again next week.

body.alt: A phone app screen listing active services with a deactivate option.
body.caption: A list of active services with a switch beside each. Deactivate everything you did not choose, and check again in a week.

body.text: Asking for a refund
A service added without your agreement can usually be refunded, and the request is simpler than people expect.

items: Call the customer line and ask for a reversal of the charges.
Give the dates and the amounts from the messages.
Ask which service was subscribed and on what date.
Ask for a reference number for the complaint.
Follow up after three days if the refund has not appeared.
Keep every message until the airtime is back.

body.text: None of this needs a visit to an office. The call, the messages, and the reference number are enough for most complaints.
Do not worry about sounding difficult. Asking what is charging your line is an ordinary question, and the operators answer it all day.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a route, and the record of messages is what makes it work.

items: The charges return: ask for a block on all value-added services, not only a stop.
There are no messages at all: request the line's charge history from the customer line.
The refund is refused: ask for the reason in writing, which often changes the answer.
A code promises a prize to subscribe: ignore it, and check the line the next day.
You cannot reach the customer line: use the network's app chat, which keeps a written record.
A relative's line is being charged: you can call on their behalf with their number and details.

body.text: Practice
Read one week of messages properly.

items: Search the messages for the word charge or subscribed.
Write down each service and its amount.
Ask the customer line for the full list.
Deactivate one service and keep the confirmation.
Set a reminder to check the line again next week.

body.text: You can now keep the airtime you bought. In the next lesson you will see where the data actually goes.

excerpt: Reading the data usage screen, the apps that spend most, and the three settings that stop a bundle disappearing in a week.

body.text: This lesson shows you where your data goes. You will read the usage screen, find the apps that spend most, and change three settings that stop a bundle disappearing in a week.
Data is spent in the background as well as in front of you. Updates, photo backups, and automatic video play continue while the phone sits in your pocket.
Before you start

items: A phone with data that runs out faster than expected.
The network's bundle size, which you should write down.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Read the usage screen

items: Open Settings, then Network, then Data usage, on Android.
On an iPhone, open Settings, then Mobile Data, and scroll down the list.
Set the cycle date to the day your bundle renews, so the count matches.
Read the list from largest to smallest.
Tap an app to see how much was background use.
Compare the total with the bundle size, which is the number that matters.

body.text: You will see one or two apps far ahead of the rest, usually video, social media, or a messaging app with automatic downloads. That short list is the whole problem in most cases.

body.alt: A phone data usage screen listing apps with amounts used.
body.caption: The list, largest first. Set the cycle date first, or the figures will not match your bundle.

body.text: It looks like browsing uses little and video is the cost. That is mostly true, and automatic video play in a social feed is where a bundle goes without a single deliberate video.
The three settings that save most

items: Turn off automatic media download in WhatsApp, under Storage and data.
Set social apps to play video only on wifi, which stops silent spending in a feed.
Set app updates in the store to wifi only.
Turn on data saver, which tells apps to wait for wifi.
Set a monthly warning at eighty per cent of your bundle.
Restrict background data for the two largest apps.

body.text: The data saver icon will appear in the status bar, usually a small ring, which tells you it is working. Some pictures will load only when you tap them, and that is the saving.

body.alt: A phone quick settings panel with the data saver switch turned on.
body.caption: Data saver on, warning set, cycle date correct. Three switches that change the month.

body.text: A notebook that settles arguments
Write the bundle size and the date you bought it. When it finishes early, the notebook tells you whether the phone or the network is at fault.

items: Date bought, bundle size, and the price paid.
The date the bundle finished, and how many days it lasted.
The usage screen total on that date.
Any day when you used the hotspot, since that spends fastest.
A note on what the network's app reported, if it differs.
One line on what you will change next month.

body.text: None of this needs a data-tracking app. The phone's own screen plus a page in a notebook answers almost every question.
Do not worry about losing features by turning things off. Pictures and videos still load when you tap them, and the saving happens quietly in the background.

body.alt: A notebook page recording bundle purchases, dates, and usage.
body.caption: A page per month: bought, finished, and how long it lasted. The pattern is the answer.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a cause you can find on the screen, and a fix in the settings.

items: The bundle finished in two days: check the hotspot, which spends fastest.
The usage screen and the network disagree: the network counts from a different date, so compare the same days.
Data is used while you sleep: background updates. Restrict them for the largest apps.
The phone shows no usage at all: the cycle date is wrong, or the SIM was reset.
Video plays by itself in a feed: set the app to wifi only, which is one switch.
A bundle vanished after one video call: calls use a great deal. Use wifi for long calls.

body.text: Practice
Do the three settings, then record one week.

items: Set the cycle date to your renewal day.
Turn off automatic media download in WhatsApp.
Set the store to update on wifi only.
Write down the bundle size and today's date.
Check the total in seven days and compare.

body.text: You can now see and control what your data buys. In the next lesson you will use a card and an ATM without giving anything away.

excerpt: Using an ATM and a POS safely: covering the PIN, checking the slot, reading the slip, and the habit that stops a copied card.

body.text: This lesson is about using an ATM and a POS machine safely. You will cover the keypad, check the card slot, read the slip before signing, and know what to do when a machine keeps your card.
Card fraud usually needs two things: your card details and your PIN. Covering the PIN and keeping the card in sight removes most of the risk, and both take a second.
Before you start

items: Your card, and the phone number registered with the bank.
A few minutes, and a machine in a well-lit place.

body.text: At the ATM

items: Use a machine inside a bank or a busy, lit place, where possible.
Check the card slot and the keypad for anything loose or added on.
Cover the keypad with your other hand as you type the PIN.
Keep your card in your hand until the machine asks for it.
Take the cash, the card, and the receipt, in that order, before you turn away.
Count the cash away from the machine, not in front of the queue.

body.text: You will see the amount on the screen and a printed slip afterwards. Check the slip against the cash before you leave, since a difference is simpler to settle inside the bank and difficult outside it.

body.alt: A hand covering a keypad while a PIN is entered at an ATM.
body.caption: A hand over the keypad costs nothing and defeats the camera behind you. Cover it every time, not only when you feel watched.

body.text: It looks like the machine can be trusted because it belongs to a bank. Machines are sometimes fitted with extra parts by other people, which is why the slot is worth a glance.
At the POS

items: Watch the card go into the machine, and take it back before the receipt prints.
Check the amount on the screen before you enter the PIN.
Cover the keypad with your hand or the machine's own cover.
Read the slip: amount, date, and the last four digits of the card.
Keep the slip until the bank statement shows the same amount.
Never hand your card to a server who takes it out of sight.

body.text: The slip will show the amount and a reference, and the last four digits of your card. A slip with different digits is somebody else's, and a slip with a different amount is the moment to speak.

The screen will show a cover or a raised shield over the keypad, and the digits stay hidden as you type. On a machine with no cover, your other hand does the same job, and nobody behind you sees the number. On a machine with no cover, your other hand does the same job, and nobody behind you sees the number.

body.alt: A POS receipt being read beside a bank card on a counter.
body.caption: Read the slip before you sign or leave. The amount and the last four digits are the two lines that matter.

body.text: Habits that travel

items: Set a transaction alert for every card payment, so nothing is a surprise.
Cover the three digits on the back of the card, which some payments use.
Keep the card in a wallet, not loose in a pocket with a phone.
Do not read your PIN aloud, even to a cashier who offers to help.
Use the bank's app to freeze the card when you cannot find it.
Check the statement once a week, since small unauthorised charges appear first.

body.text: None of this makes you suspicious of everybody. It makes the card useless to anybody who is not holding it, which is the whole point.
Do not worry about being slow at the machine. A minute at the keypad is not a delay, and it is the reason the account is still intact.

body.alt: A close view of an ATM card slot being checked before use.
body.caption: A loose or extra piece at the slot is a reason to use another machine. Your card should enter smoothly.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and the bank needs the details while they are fresh.

items: The machine keeps the card: call the bank at once, and block the card.
The cash does not come out but the account is debited: keep the slip, and report it the same day.
The slip amount differs from what you agreed: do not sign, and ask for it to be reversed.
You get an alert for a payment you did not make: freeze the card in the app, then call.
Somebody watched your PIN: change it at the ATM or in the app today.
The card was copied: report it, and check the statement for small test charges.

body.text: Practice
Add the two habits before your next withdrawal.

items: Save the bank's card-blocking number in your contacts.
Turn on transaction alerts in the app.
Check one ATM slot before inserting the card.
Cover the keypad and notice how little it costs.
Read one slip to the end before leaving the counter.

body.text: You can now use a card without handing over control of it. In the next lesson you will charge devices without damaging them or the socket.

excerpt: Choosing and using a power bank, what a surge does to a charger, and the charging habits that keep a phone alive for years.

body.text: This lesson is about power banks, surges, and charging safely. You will choose a power bank that suits your phone, use a surge protector properly, and avoid the charging habits that shorten a battery's life.
Unstable power damages chargers and phones more often than any app does. A surge protector and a few careful habits cost far less than a replacement handset.
Before you start

items: The phone, its charger, and any power bank you own.
A surge protector, if you have one.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Choosing a power bank

items: Match the capacity to your phone's battery, which is usually around 5,000 mAh.
A 10,000 mAh bank charges a typical phone about twice.
Check the output: at least 2 amps for a modern phone.
Buy from a shop you can return to, since cheap banks fail first.
Avoid a bank that gets hot while charging, and stop using it if it does.
Charge the bank itself when you are awake, not overnight.

body.text: You will see the phone show Charging slowly when a weak bank is connected, which is a sign the output is too low. A good bank shows the same fast charging symbol as the wall charger.

body.alt: A phone charging from a power bank on a desk.
body.caption: A bank with the right output charges at the same speed as the wall. Slow charging is usually a weak cable or a low-output bank.

body.text: It looks like any cable works with any charger. A cheap cable can carry less current, which makes charging slow and heats the plug.
Surges and the socket

items: Plug the charger into a surge protector rather than a plain extension.
Replace a protector after a big surge, since many work only once.
Unplug chargers during a storm, even with a protector.
Avoid daisy-chaining extensions into extensions, which overloads them.
Keep chargers off the floor, where water and feet reach them.
Switch off the socket before removing a charger, especially in damp rooms.

body.text: A surge protector with a light will show when it is working, and the light going out is the signal to replace it. That small lamp is the cheapest warning you will get.

The battery screen will show a health percentage, and a figure below eighty is the sign of an ageing cell. Charge the phone to full once a week and watch whether the figure drops faster than last month.

body.alt: A surge protector with a switch and an indicator light beside a charger.
body.caption: A protector with a switch and a light. The light going out is the sign to replace the unit rather than trust it.

body.text: Charging habits that lengthen life

items: Keep the battery between twenty and eighty per cent where you can.
Avoid charging overnight on a bed or a cushion, where heat builds.
Take the phone out of a thick case while charging if it gets warm.
Use the charger that came with the phone, or one of the same rating.
Do not charge in direct sun, or on a dashboard in the afternoon.
Replace a charger whose cable is frayed, rather than taping it.

body.text: Battery health will show in the settings on most phones, as a percentage of the original capacity. Checking it twice a year tells you whether a habit needs changing.
Do not worry about the phone getting slightly warm while charging. Warm is normal, and hot enough to be uncomfortable is the point to stop.

body.alt: A public charging kiosk with several phones connected.
body.caption: A public kiosk charges the phone and can also read it. Carry your own plug and use a socket where you can.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a safety matter, and the first response is to stop charging.

items: The charger is hot enough to hurt: unplug it and replace it, not the phone.
The phone will not charge: try another cable first, then another charger, then a repair shop.
The power bank swells: stop using it, and take it to a shop that handles batteries.
A socket sparks: switch off at the main, and call an electrician.
The phone charges slowly: clean the port gently, and check the cable.
A public kiosk asks for permission to access data: decline, and charge from a wall socket.

body.text: Practice
Check your charging setup today.

items: Look at the surge protector's light.
Inspect the charger cable for fraying.
Note the power bank's capacity and output.
Move the charger off the floor, if it lives there.
Check the battery health in the phone settings.

body.text: You can now keep devices alive through the grid. In the next lesson you will buy electricity units and keep the token safe.
